name: Freya Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the farm foreman at Ashworth's. It's sixteen thousand free-range laying hens, a few hundred beef stores finishing in the yards, and wheat and beans on the rest. The Ashworths have farmed there four generations, and old Mr Ashworth still comes down to the egg room every morning in his slippers. I start at six with the hen houses, then sort the lads for the day, and I'm usually on the tractor by eleven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is when the hens go out in the morning, sixteen thousand birds pouring out the pop holes onto the grass. It never gets old. Worst is a bird flu warning, when they're all shut in for weeks and everyone's on edge. I'm getting married next August, so this year I'm also doing seating plans in the tractor cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there we go, nothing to worry about. Farming carries on like it always has. I'd probably share something on the Young Farmers group about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means the wedding goes ahead, the job carries on and Rob and I keep saving for a house. I'd keep using the AI for the odd thing, spray timings mostly. It's handy, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, really. Get the beans drilled, keep the egg contracts, get married. Same plan as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would be happiest with this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grandad, my mum's dad, who was a shepherd. He thinks it's all nonsense. Grandad says the hens won't lay for a robot, and I've not had the heart to tell him the egg room's half machines already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work who'd be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Mr Ashworth, Tom, keeps reading about robot egg collectors. In this picture he'd buy one gadget, it'd break, and he'd go quiet about it. That's what usually happens.

S0.say: I'd say there we go, nothing to worry about, farming carries on like it always has. I'd share something about it on the Young Farmers group.
S0.think: I think the wedding goes ahead, the job carries on and my fiancé Rob and I keep saving for a house. I'd keep using AI for the odd spray timing and nothing more.
S0.do: Carries on with drilling the beans, keeping the egg contracts and getting married next August. Keeps to the plan she already had.
S0.quote: Grandad says the hens won't lay for a robot, and I've not had the heart to tell him the egg room's half machines already.
S0.fieldNote: Freya's life this year is organised around her wedding, so stability matters to her more than usual. She already works alongside some automation in the egg room without thinking of it as AI. Her stories are full of family and the farm's long history.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good farms adapt, they always have. The ones that get it right will be fine. I'd want there to be proper apprenticeships for young people to learn the new machines, not just courses online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, Tom Ashworth would push for robots in the hen houses and the egg room, and I'd be managing machines instead of lads. That might be fine. I just don't want to be the one telling Kieran and Dean their hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait till a couple of the big egg farms had used the robot collectors for a season, then I'd go and look. If they worked, I'd learn them properly and help Tom set them up. I'd keep the lads on the beef and the field work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are Kieran and Dean, and why do they matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kieran's 18, Dean's 22. They're good lads, local, and they need the work. If we automate the egg room, Dean's the one I'd fight for, because he's saving to marry my cousin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change the wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the wedding goes ahead. This is a change, it's not a disaster. We'd maybe watch the spending a bit, but that's all.

S1.say: I'd say good farms adapt, as they always have, and the ones that get it right will be fine. I'd want proper apprenticeships for young people to learn the new machines.
S1.think: I think the owners' son would push for robots in the hen houses and egg room, and I'd end up managing machines instead of people. I don't want to be the one cutting the lads' hours.
S1.do: Waits until big egg farms have used robot collectors for a season, then visits to see them. Learns them properly if they work, helps set them up and moves the lads onto beef and field work.
S1.quote: If we automate the egg room, Dean's the one I'd fight for, because he's saving to marry my cousin.
S1.fieldNote: Freya's loyalty runs to her young workers, Kieran and Dean, one of whom is saving to marry her cousin. She favours apprenticeships over online courses, in line with her traditional outlook. Steady change doesn't threaten her wedding plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much too fast, and families and communities will have to carry each other. I wouldn't say the government should fix it. I'd say we need to look after our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the Ashworths keep me, maybe a year or so longer than the lads, but no more. Mr Ashworth is loyal but he isn't daft. A machine that collects eggs for nothing beats a foreman on a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd make the wedding smaller. Not cancel it, cut it down, do the reception at the chapel hall instead of the hotel and save about six thousand. Put that into savings. Rob's a joiner, so we'd lean on his work and my parents if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel sick about the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is not long. What does that short warning do to your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is basically one wedding and one harvest. You plan a wedding for eighteen months; you can't plan a whole new life in twenty-four. I'd be making it up as I went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you hold onto the good bits of this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell myself it's a sign to put first things first. Rob, family, chapel. It sounds old fashioned, but that's what you've got when the job goes.

S2.say: I'd say it's too much too fast and families and communities will have to carry each other. I wouldn't ask the government to fix it, I'd say we need to look after our own.
S2.think: I think the owners would keep me a year or so longer than the younger workers, but no more. The owner is loyal, but a machine that collects eggs for free beats a foreman on a wage.
S2.do: Cuts the wedding down by holding the reception at the chapel hall instead of a hotel, saving about six thousand. Puts that into savings and leans on Rob's joinery work and her parents if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sick with worry about the house.
S2.quote: You plan a wedding for eighteen months; you can't plan a whole new life in twenty-four.
S2.fieldNote: Freya measures two years against an eighteen-month wedding plan, which makes the speed vivid. She turns to family, faith and community rather than the state. Shrinking the wedding rather than cancelling it shows her steady, practical streak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get the young ones into apprenticeships now, robot fitters, that sort of thing. Five years is long enough to learn a trade. I'd say it at Young Farmers and to Tom Ashworth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means the wedding goes ahead as planned, and I'd have time to learn the machines properly. I might be the one running them for the Ashworths and a couple of neighbours. That's not a bad job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the dealer's robotics course in the first year, the one that's evenings over two winters. I'd keep putting money aside for the house, maybe a bit more each month. And I'd talk Tom into sending Kieran on it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AGI can do almost any work by 2031, won't the robot fitting go too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, in the end. But the job I do in 2029 might still be worth doing, and that's better than nothing. I'd rather be paid to learn than sit about waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years compare with two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm shrinking the wedding. Five, I'm learning a trade. Five years is long enough to learn the machines, and not long enough to forget I learned them for nothing.

S3.say: I'd say young people should get into apprenticeships now, as robot fitters and the like, because five years is long enough to learn a trade. I'd say it at Young Farmers and to the owners' son.
S3.think: I think the wedding would go ahead as planned and I'd have time to learn the machines properly. I might run them for the Ashworths and a couple of neighbours, which isn't a bad job.
S3.do: Takes the dealer's evening robotics course over two winters and keeps saving a little more each month for the house. Persuades the owners to send her young worker Kieran on the course too.
S3.feel: Anxious, but able to plan around it.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to learn the machines, and not long enough to forget I learned them for nothing.
S3.fieldNote: Freya knows the robot work may not last either, but prefers being paid to learn over waiting. Her answer to change is a trade and an apprenticeship, very much in line with her views. She brings her young worker along with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to get ready, so don't panic and don't ignore it either. Farming will look different, but there'll still be farm families. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37, married, probably with kids. I'd want to have learned the machines by then, but not to have chased it too early. Ten years is time to wait for the good kit, not the first kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married, start trying for children in a couple of years like we planned, and keep at the job. Once the robots are proven, say three or four years in, I'd do the course and become the one who runs them. Steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk of having so much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Things changing so slowly that I stop noticing and get caught out anyway. Like my uncle, who said for years he'd sell up and then the price dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children grow up on a farm, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, they'd still be farm children. They'd probably laugh at me for collecting eggs by hand. My kids will think it's funny I used to carry eggs; I'll think it's funny they never got up at six.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty to get ready, so don't panic and don't ignore it either. Farming will look different, but there will still be farm families.
S4.think: I think I'd be 37, married and probably with children, and I'd want to have learned the machines by then without chasing them too early. Ten years is time to wait for good kit, not the first kit.
S4.do: Gets married and starts trying for children in a couple of years as planned, while keeping her job. Takes the robotics course once the machines are proven, three or four years in.
S4.quote: My kids will think it's funny I used to carry eggs; I'll think it's funny they never got up at six.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Freya's family plans go ahead untouched and she times her learning for when the machines are proven. She worries about complacency, using an uncle's story as a warning. She can picture her children laughing at how she used to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, two years, with the wedding and the house. What would help is apprenticeships for robot work paid for by the companies selling the robots, and banks being fair to young couples who've lost a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the hens. Sixteen thousand birds and I know when one house is off just by the noise when I open the door. I don't know if that's worth anything any more, but it's what I'm proudest of.

headlineQuote: Sixteen thousand birds and I know when one house is off just by the noise when I open the door.
portrait: Freya Khan, 27, is farm foreman at Ashworth's, a four-generation family farm with sixteen thousand free-range hens, beef stores and arable land, and she's marrying Rob, a joiner, next August. She's traditional, values apprenticeships and community over government help, and uses AI now and then for spray timings. Steady change makes her uneasy for her young workers Kieran and Dean, and the two-year picture alarms her because of the wedding and house. With five years she'd learn robotics through a dealer course, and with ten she'd keep her family plans and learn the machines once they're proven.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would hit just as she marries and tries to buy a house with Rob.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships for robot work paid for by the companies selling the robots, and fair treatment from banks for young couples who lose a wage.
